about: One of the largest power producers in the US. It owns natural gas, nuclear, coal, solar and battery plants, and it also sells electricity directly to homes and businesses.
revenue: It makes money two ways. It sells electricity and capacity from its plants into the wholesale power markets, and it sells electricity to millions of retail customers under brands such as TXU Energy. More and more of its output is sold years ahead on long-term contracts, including deals with tech companies that need around-the-clock power for data centers.
segments: Retail electricity · Wholesale power generation · Nuclear fleet · Long-term power contracts

about: An advertising technology company. Its AI-driven ad engine, called AXON, decides which ads to show inside mobile apps and games.
revenue: Advertisers, mostly mobile game makers and increasingly online shops, pay to show ads through AppLovin's platform, and AppLovin keeps a share of that spend. It sold its own mobile games business in 2025 to focus on advertising.
segments: Mobile app advertising · E-commerce advertising · Ad marketplace for app publishers

about: The largest independent company that maintains and overhauls aircraft engines. Its customers are airlines, the military and business jet operators.
revenue: It charges to take engines apart, repair or replace parts and rebuild them, which every engine needs regularly by rule. Much of the work runs on multi-year agreements with engine makers and operators, so revenue tends to repeat.
segments: Engine overhaul services · Component repair · Commercial, military and business aviation

about: A large chip and software company. It designs custom AI chips for the biggest cloud companies, along with networking, broadband and wireless chips. Through acquisitions such as VMware, it also sells software to large businesses.
revenue: About half its sales come from chips sold to cloud providers, phone makers and network equipment companies. Custom AI accelerators and data-center networking are the fastest-growing part. The rest comes from software licenses and subscriptions, mainly VMware, sold to large enterprises.
segments: Custom AI chips · Networking chips · Broadband and wireless chips · Infrastructure software (VMware)

about: The largest online pet store in the US. It sells pet food, treats, supplies and medications, and it also runs its own vet clinics.
revenue: Most of its money comes from selling pet products online. Most sales arrive through Autoship, where customers get repeat deliveries on a schedule. It also earns from its pet pharmacy, vet care, ads that brands pay to place on its site, and the paid Chewy+ membership.
segments: Pet food and supplies · Autoship subscriptions · Pet pharmacy · Vet clinics · Sponsored ads

about: The world's largest pest control company. In the US it owns Terminix. It also provides washroom and hygiene services to businesses.
revenue: It charges homes and businesses (restaurants, warehouses, hospitals, food plants) for regular pest control visits, usually on recurring contracts. Hygiene services such as washroom supplies and cleaning also run on contracts. That makes most of its revenue repeat business.
segments: Pest control (incl. Terminix) · Hygiene and wellbeing · Workwear (France)

about: One of the largest aerospace and defense companies. It is made up of Collins Aerospace (aircraft systems), Pratt & Whitney (jet engines) and Raytheon (missiles, radars and air defense such as Patriot).
revenue: It sells engines and aircraft parts to plane makers and airlines, and earns a lot from spare parts and servicing engines already flying. It also sells missiles, radars and defense systems to the US government and allied countries under long contracts.
segments: Commercial aerospace parts and aftermarket · Jet engines · Missiles and air defense

about: One of the world's two big passenger-jet makers, with the 737 and 787. It is also a major defense and space contractor.
revenue: Most revenue comes from selling commercial airplanes to airlines, paid largely on delivery. It also sells fighter jets, tankers, helicopters, satellites and missile parts to the US and allied governments. A services arm earns from spare parts, maintenance and training for planes already in service.
segments: Commercial airplanes · Defense, space and security · Global services

about: A government technology contractor. It builds and runs IT, software, cyber and intelligence systems for US defense and intelligence agencies.
revenue: Almost all of its revenue comes from US federal government contracts. It is paid to deliver technology, engineering and mission support, often on multi-year contracts that run on a cost-plus or fixed-price basis.
segments: Defense and intelligence technology · Cyber and electronic warfare · Federal IT services

about: The only large-scale rare earth miner in the US. It owns the Mountain Pass mine in California and is building a plant in Texas to make rare earth magnets.
revenue: It sells rare earth materials mined and processed at Mountain Pass, especially the NdPr used in magnets for electric motors, wind turbines and defense systems. It is adding sales of finished magnets. A 2025 agreement with the US Defense Department guarantees a minimum price for its NdPr.
segments: Rare earth concentrate · Separated NdPr oxide · Rare earth magnets

about: The largest military shipbuilder in the US. It is the only company that builds the Navy's aircraft carriers, and one of two that build its nuclear submarines.
revenue: Nearly all of its revenue comes from US Navy and Coast Guard contracts to design, build, refuel and overhaul ships, which take years each. A smaller technology arm sells unmanned systems, cyber and IT services to the government.
segments: Aircraft carriers and submarines (Newport News) · Amphibious ships and destroyers (Ingalls) · Mission technologies

about: A defense technology company that makes jet-powered drones, including target drones and the XQ-58 Valkyrie combat drone. It also makes small jet engines, rocket and hypersonic test systems, and satellite communications equipment.
revenue: Most of its revenue comes from US military and allied government contracts. It sells drones, engines and systems, and runs test and training services. It often funds new products itself and then sells them at volume, instead of waiting for the government to pay for development.
segments: Drones (unmanned systems) · Jet engines · Hypersonics and rockets · Satellite communications

about: One of the largest cybersecurity companies. It protects business networks, cloud systems and employee devices from hackers.
revenue: It sells firewalls (hardware and software) and, increasingly, subscriptions to its security software for networks (Strata), cloud (Prisma) and security operations (Cortex). Most revenue now repeats through subscriptions and support contracts that businesses renew each year.
segments: Network security and firewalls · Cloud security · Security operations · Subscriptions and support

about: A consumer cybersecurity company behind the brands Norton, Avast, AVG, Avira and LifeLock. It protects people's devices, identities and privacy.
revenue: Most of its money comes from consumers paying yearly subscriptions for antivirus, VPN, identity-theft protection and privacy tools, most of which renew automatically. In 2025 it bought MoneyLion, which adds income from consumer finance products.
segments: Device security (Norton, Avast) · Identity protection (LifeLock) · Privacy and VPN · Consumer finance (MoneyLion)

about: Owns the New York Stock Exchange and a global group of futures and options markets. It also runs big mortgage-technology and bond-data businesses.
revenue: It charges fees every time something trades on its venues, and it sells the price data and analytics that come off those venues. A third leg sells software that banks use to originate and service US mortgages, which brings in steady subscription revenue.
segments: Exchanges · Fixed income and data services · Mortgage technology

about: The owner of Burger King, Tim Hortons, Popeyes and Firehouse Subs. Almost all of its roughly 32,000 restaurants are run by franchisees.
revenue: It takes a royalty on what each franchised restaurant sells, plus rent on properties it leases to them and fees when a new restaurant opens. Because franchisees carry the operating costs, most of the royalty falls through as profit.
segments: Burger King · Tim Hortons · Popeyes · Firehouse Subs

about: A contractor that physically builds telecom networks: burying fibre, installing cable and wiring up data centres across the US.
revenue: Telecom carriers and, increasingly, data-centre operators hire it on multi-year master service agreements. It is paid for the engineering and construction work it completes, so revenue tracks how much the carriers and hyperscalers are spending on new network capacity.
segments: Fibre construction · Engineering services · Maintenance and locating · Data-centre networks

about: The largest US online sportsbook, with a casino app alongside it. It operates in most states that have legalised online betting.
revenue: It keeps a slice of everything wagered — the margin between the odds it offers and the true probability — and takes a house edge on casino games. Marketing and promotional credits to win customers are the big cost against that.
segments: Online sportsbook · iGaming casino · Daily fantasy sports

about: Makes a very large catalogue of small, highly specified aircraft parts — pumps, valves, latches, ignition systems — most of which it is the only approved supplier for.
revenue: It sells parts to aircraft makers at thin margins, then earns most of its profit over the following decades selling replacements into the aftermarket, where being the sole certified source gives it pricing power.
segments: Power and control · Airframe components · Aftermarket spares

about: The largest US manufacturer of printed circuit boards cleared for defence work, and a growing supplier of boards for AI data centres.
revenue: Defence primes and electronics makers pay it to design and manufacture circuit boards and radio-frequency components to order. Defence programmes give it long, funded production runs, while the data-centre side sells high-layer-count boards for AI servers.
segments: Defence and aerospace boards · RF components · Data-centre networking boards

about: One of the biggest medical-device makers, best known for artificial hips and knees, surgical power tools and hospital beds.
revenue: Hospitals buy its implants and instruments, and it sells the disposable items and service contracts that go with them. Its surgical robot is placed in hospitals partly to lock in the implants used with it.
segments: Orthopaedic implants · Surgical equipment · Neurotechnology and spine · Medical-surgical supplies

about: A biotech focused on drugs for brain and hormone disorders. Its main product treats tardive dyskinesia, an involuntary movement disorder.
revenue: It sells its approved medicines through US specialty pharmacies and collects royalties on drugs partners sell abroad. Nearly all revenue comes from a small number of branded products, so patent life and new approvals matter a great deal.
segments: Movement disorders · Endocrinology · Neuropsychiatry pipeline

about: Makes devices used inside the body: heart stents, catheters that treat irregular heartbeats, pacemakers and urology tools.
revenue: Hospitals buy the devices case by case, and most are single-use, so revenue repeats with procedure volumes. Its fastest-growing line is electrophysiology, the catheters used to treat atrial fibrillation.
segments: Cardiology · Electrophysiology · Endoscopy · Urology

about: A South Korean memory-chip maker and, with Samsung and Micron, one of three companies that supply most of the world's DRAM. It is the leading supplier of the high-bandwidth memory stacked next to AI accelerators.
revenue: It sells memory chips by the wafer-load to server builders, phone makers and AI chip companies. Prices swing hard with supply and demand, so profits can move far more than revenue; the high-bandwidth memory used in AI systems is sold out well ahead on contract.
segments: DRAM · High-bandwidth memory · NAND flash

about: One of the largest alternative asset managers, buying companies, lending to them and owning infrastructure and property on behalf of pensions and insurers. It also owns an insurance company.
revenue: It charges a management fee on the money it looks after and keeps a share of the investment profit above a hurdle. A growing part of earnings is simply the return on its own capital invested alongside clients and on its insurance balance sheet.
segments: Private equity · Credit · Infrastructure and real assets · Insurance

about: Owns and leases jet engines, and increasingly repairs and sells engine modules rather than whole engines.
revenue: Airlines pay it rent on leased engines and aircraft. Its faster-growing business buys used engines, strips them into modules, overhauls those and sells or swaps them back to airlines, which is cheaper for the airline than a full shop visit and more profitable for FTAI.
segments: Engine leasing · Module swaps and repair · Aircraft leasing

about: A large US infrastructure contractor that builds power lines, pipelines, telecom networks and renewable-energy plants.
revenue: Utilities, telecom carriers and energy companies award it construction contracts, mostly on a unit-price or fixed-fee basis. Earnings depend on the pace of grid, pipeline and network spending and on how well it estimates job costs.
segments: Power delivery · Pipeline infrastructure · Communications · Clean energy

about: Sells cloud software that handles the money side of American health care: checking insurance, submitting claims and chasing payment.
revenue: Hospitals and physician groups pay recurring subscription and per-transaction fees. Because the software sits in the billing workflow, revenue scales with how many claims flow through it and is hard to displace once installed.
segments: Claims management · Patient payments · Denial and appeal tools · Revenue analytics

about: Makes basic clothing — T-shirts, fleece, socks and underwear — in its own factories in Central America and the Caribbean.
revenue: Most sales go to wholesalers who print logos on blank garments for events and uniforms, and the rest go to retailers under its own and licensed brands. Owning the factories keeps costs low, so profit turns on cotton prices and how full the plants are.
segments: Activewear blanks · Socks and underwear · Licensed and private brands

about: A mid-sized miner of gold and silver with operations in the United States, Mexico and Canada.
revenue: It digs ore, processes it into metal and sells that at prevailing gold and silver prices. It has no control over the price it receives, so profit depends on keeping the cost per ounce below the market price and on how much it can mine.
segments: Gold mining · Silver mining · Exploration

about: The largest US provider of contract compression — the big compressor packages that push natural gas through gathering systems and pipelines.
revenue: Producers rent the compressors on multi-year fixed-fee contracts and Kodiak operates and maintains them. Because gas has to be compressed whatever the price, the revenue is steadier than most oilfield-services work.
segments: Contract compression · Station construction · Maintenance services

about: Nubank, the largest digital bank in Latin America, with the bulk of its customers in Brazil and growing operations in Mexico and Colombia. It has no branches.
revenue: It earns interest on credit-card balances and personal loans, takes interchange fees when customers pay by card, and earns a spread on deposits. Running without branches keeps the cost of serving each customer very low, which is where most of the profit comes from.
segments: Credit cards · Personal lending · Deposits and savings · Investments and insurance

about: Listed on NASDAQ under the ticker HAPN. The post names it only as "Happen" among DeepSeek's buys and gives no description, and this entry has not been verified against company filings.
revenue: Not established from the post. DeepSeek's stated reason for the whole basket was price: cheap earnings multiples rather than anything specific to this business.
segments: Not confirmed

about: A specialty insurer that writes coverage standard insurers avoid, such as energy operations, farms, professional liability and specialty accident and health.
revenue: It earns premiums on niche policies and invests the float. Since January it also owns a Lloyd's business that earns fees without tying up its own capital.
segments: Specialty property and casualty · Accident and health · Agriculture · Lloyd's

about: Southeast Asia's largest internet group: the Shopee online marketplace, the Garena games business and the Monee digital-finance arm.
revenue: Shopee earns commissions, ads and logistics fees on goods sold through it. Garena sells in-game items, mainly in Free Fire. Monee earns interest and fees on consumer and merchant loans and payments.
segments: Shopee (e-commerce) · Garena (games) · Monee (digital finance)

about: The second-largest US wireless carrier by subscribers, with a large 5G network and a growing home-internet business.
revenue: Most revenue is monthly phone and data plans; it also sells handsets and fixed wireless home internet.
segments: Postpaid wireless · Prepaid wireless · Home internet · Equipment

about: The largest US retail brokerage and a major custodian for independent financial advisers.
revenue: Much of its income is interest earned on clients' cash swept into its bank. It also earns asset-management fees on its funds and trading revenue.
segments: Investor services · Advisor services · Banking · Asset management

about: A cross-border payments company that lets people and businesses send, hold and spend money in many currencies at close to the mid-market rate.
revenue: It charges a small, visible fee on each transfer or currency conversion, and earns interest on customer balances. Card and business accounts add more fee income.
segments: Personal transfers · Business accounts · Wise Platform (for banks)

about: Makes smart meters, sensors and the network software utilities use to measure and manage electricity, gas and water.
revenue: Utilities buy its meters and network hardware, then pay recurring fees for software, data and managed services over long contracts.
segments: Device solutions · Networked solutions · Outcomes (software and services)

about: One of the largest US defense contractors, building the B-21 bomber, the Sentinel ICBM, satellites and missile defense systems.
revenue: Almost all revenue comes from long government contracts, mainly with the US Department of Defense.
segments: Aeronautics · Defense systems · Mission systems · Space systems

about: Runs one of the largest content-delivery networks and sells edge security that protects websites and apps from attacks, plus a growing cloud-computing business.
revenue: Customers pay recurring fees based on traffic and services used for delivering content, blocking attacks and running workloads on its cloud.
segments: Security · Content delivery · Cloud computing

about: Ultra Clean Holdings supplies critical subsystems, components and parts that go inside the machines used to make semiconductors, and cleans and analyses those parts for chipmakers.
revenue: Most revenue comes from selling gas delivery systems and other subsystems to chip-equipment makers such as Lam Research and Applied Materials, so sales rise and fall with spending on new fab tools. A smaller services business earns recurring fees for cleaning and coating parts used in chip factories.
segments: Semiconductor subsystems · Gas delivery systems · Parts cleaning and analytics services

sector: Oil and gas exploration and production
about: Devon Energy is a large US independent oil and gas producer with most of its output from the Delaware Basin in Texas and New Mexico.
revenue: It earns money by producing and selling crude oil, natural gas and natural gas liquids, so its profits move with commodity prices. It returns much of its cash flow to shareholders through a fixed-plus-variable dividend and buybacks.
segments: Delaware Basin · Eagle Ford · Anadarko Basin · Williston Basin · Powder River Basin

about: An engineering and technology contractor that does most of its work for the US and allied governments, from space and defense support to military logistics. It also licenses chemical and refining process technology, and it plans to split into two companies.
revenue: Most revenue comes from long government contracts for engineering, science, IT and support services. The smaller technology arm earns licence fees, proprietary equipment sales and consulting on ammonia, refining and chemical plants.
segments: Government and defense services · Space and intelligence work · Process technology licensing

about: The largest natural gas producer in the US, formed in 2024 when Chesapeake Energy combined with Southwestern Energy. Its wells are in the Appalachian Basin and the Haynesville shale of Louisiana and Texas.
revenue: It sells natural gas, plus some oil and natural gas liquids, so its profits rise and fall with gas prices; hedges smooth part of that. It returns cash through a base dividend plus buybacks or variable payouts.
segments: Marcellus and Utica (Appalachia) · Haynesville · Gas marketing

about: The leading developer of RNA interference (RNAi) medicines, which silence the genes that make disease-causing proteins. Its biggest franchise treats transthyretin (TTR) amyloidosis, which damages the heart and nerves.
revenue: It sells its own drugs, led by Amvuttra and Onpattro for TTR amyloidosis, plus Givlaari and Oxlumo for rare liver and kidney diseases. It also earns royalties and milestones from partners, including Novartis on the cholesterol drug Leqvio.
segments: TTR amyloidosis (Amvuttra, Onpattro) · Rare disease drugs · Partner royalties · RNAi pipeline

about: The sole maker of nuclear reactors and reactor fuel for US Navy submarines and aircraft carriers. It also makes parts for commercial nuclear plants and medical isotopes, and runs nuclear sites for the US government.
revenue: Most revenue comes from long US government contracts for naval reactors and fuel, which give it a deep backlog. The rest comes from commercial nuclear components and services, mainly in Canada, medical radioisotopes and site-management fees.
segments: Government Operations (naval reactors and fuel) · Commercial Operations · Medical isotopes

about: Makes cloud software that large companies use to run customer interactions across social media, messaging, chat and contact centers in one place.
revenue: Most revenue is subscription fees for its platform, sold to big enterprises on multi-year contracts. A smaller share comes from implementation and other professional services.
segments: Customer service and contact center · Social listening and marketing · Insights · Professional services

about: A visual discovery site and app where people save and search images of ideas and products, used by more than 500 million people a month.
revenue: Nearly all revenue is advertising: brands and retailers pay to show promoted pins and shopping ads to people planning purchases. Most users are outside the US, but most revenue still comes from the US and Canada.
segments: Advertising · Shopping ads · US and Canada · Europe · Rest of world

about: A late-stage drug developer working on deucrictibant, an oral pill that blocks the bradykinin B2 receptor, to treat and prevent swelling attacks in hereditary angioedema (HAE) and related conditions.
revenue: It has no product sales yet and funds its research with cash raised from investors. Revenue depends on deucrictibant winning approval and selling as an on-demand and preventive HAE treatment.
segments: Deucrictibant (on-demand HAE) · Deucrictibant (HAE prevention) · Acquired angioedema

about: Makes TurboTax tax software, QuickBooks accounting software for small businesses, the Credit Karma personal-finance app and the Mailchimp email marketing service.
revenue: Most revenue comes from subscriptions and fees for QuickBooks and its add-ons such as payroll and payments, and from TurboTax filing fees, which arrive mostly in the US tax season. Credit Karma earns referral fees when members take out cards and loans.
segments: QuickBooks and Mailchimp (businesses) · TurboTax (consumers) · Credit Karma · ProTax

about: Runs the world's largest ride-hailing network and the Uber Eats food and grocery delivery service in dozens of countries, plus a freight brokerage.
revenue: It keeps a cut of each ride and delivery booked through its apps, plus fees and a growing advertising business. Uber One memberships add recurring fees.
segments: Mobility · Delivery · Freight · Advertising

about: A US oil and gas producer that has grown by buying mature, slower-declining assets, mainly in the Eagle Ford, Permian and Uinta basins. It also owns mineral and royalty interests.
revenue: It sells crude oil, natural gas and natural gas liquids, so profits move with commodity prices; hedges cover part of its output. It returns cash through dividends and buybacks.
segments: Eagle Ford · Permian Basin · Uinta Basin · Minerals and royalties

about: One of the world's larger gold miners, with mines in the Americas and West Africa, including Tasiast (Mauritania), Paracatu (Brazil), La Coipa (Chile), and Fort Knox and Round Mountain (US).
revenue: It earns money by selling the gold, and some silver, that it mines, so profit depends on the gold price minus its all-in cost per ounce.
segments: Tasiast · Paracatu · La Coipa · US mines (Fort Knox, Round Mountain, Bald Mountain) · Great Bear project

about: One of the largest makers of turbochargers for cars and trucks. It is also building electric boosting, high-speed electric motors and compressors for industrial uses.
revenue: It sells turbochargers and related parts to carmakers and truck makers worldwide, and replacement parts through the aftermarket. Newer lines sell compressors and electric motors for industrial and electrified uses.
segments: Light-vehicle turbochargers · Commercial-vehicle turbochargers · Aftermarket · Industrial compression and e-motors

about: A video platform popular with young people in China, known for anime, gaming and user-made videos with live on-screen comments.
revenue: It earns money from paid features such as premium memberships and live-streaming tips, from advertising, and from mobile games it publishes, plus some merchandise.
segments: Value-added services · Advertising · Mobile games · IP derivatives and other

about: A US government contractor formed in 2024 when Amentum merged with Jacobs' government services business. It provides engineering, technology, environmental cleanup and nuclear services to the US and allied governments.
revenue: It is paid under long government contracts for work such as intelligence analytics, space systems, cybersecurity, military platform support and nuclear site cleanup.
segments: Digital Solutions · Global Engineering Solutions

about: Develops eye medicines built on a dissolvable hydrogel that releases drug over time. Its lead candidate, AXPAXLI, is an implant for wet age-related macular degeneration in late-stage trials.
revenue: Current revenue comes from Dextenza, an eye insert for pain and inflammation after eye surgery. The bigger prize is AXPAXLI, which would compete with frequent eye injections if approved.
segments: Dextenza (on the market) · AXPAXLI (wet AMD, diabetic retinopathy) · Pipeline

about: The leading designer of graphics processors (GPUs) and the dominant supplier of the chips and systems used to train and run AI models.
revenue: Most revenue now comes from data centers: AI accelerators, full server systems and networking sold to cloud providers and large companies. Gaming graphics cards, professional visualization and automotive chips make up the rest.
segments: Data center (AI chips, networking) · Gaming · Professional visualization · Automotive

about: Runs an AI-driven performance marketing and ad monetization platform (Cortex) for mobile apps, helping app makers, especially games, find users and earn money from in-app ads.
revenue: Advertisers pay it to acquire users who install and spend in their apps, and it takes a share of the ad revenue it generates for app publishers through its in-app ad exchange and mediation tools.
segments: User acquisition (advertisers) · Ad monetization (publishers) · Gaming · Consumer apps

about: One of the world's largest contract manufacturers, building electronics and equipment for other companies, with a fast-growing business in power and cooling gear for data centers.
revenue: Customers pay it to design, source and assemble their products, from networking gear and appliances to car electronics and medical devices. Margins are thin on assembly work and higher on its own power and cooling products.
segments: Cloud and Power Infrastructure · Integrated Technology Solutions · Regulated Manufacturing Solutions

about: Supplies billing, customer-management and network software, plus long-term managed services, to telecom and media companies such as AT&T and T-Mobile.
revenue: Most revenue comes from multi-year managed-services contracts in which it runs and updates customers' systems, plus software licences and project work. A few very large telecom customers account for much of its revenue.
segments: Managed services · Billing and monetization software · Customer experience (CRM) · Cloud and network services

about: A drug developer focused on lorundrostat, a once-daily pill that blocks aldosterone production, for hard-to-control high blood pressure and kidney disease.
revenue: It has no product sales yet and funds itself with cash from investors. Revenue would come from selling lorundrostat if the FDA approves it.
segments: Lorundrostat (hypertension) · Chronic kidney disease · Obstructive sleep apnea

about: One of the largest US sellers of annuities, spun off from MetLife in 2017, with a block of life insurance policies as well. It has agreed to a $70-a-share cash takeover by Aquarian Holdings that still needs state insurance approvals.
revenue: It earns fees on the variable and index-linked annuities it sells, mostly through banks and brokers, and investment income on the money it holds until payouts come due. Life insurance premiums make up the rest.
segments: Annuities · Life insurance · Run-off policies

about: Makes axles, driveshafts, transmissions and electric drive systems for cars, trucks and commercial vehicles. It sells to vehicle makers, not to drivers.
revenue: Car and truck makers buy its drivetrain parts and electric-drive units for the vehicles they build, usually under multi-year supply contracts. It also sells seals and thermal-management parts used across many kinds of vehicles.
segments: Light-vehicle drivetrains · Commercial-vehicle drivetrains · Electric drive systems · Seals and thermal parts

about: Builds the Alpha small rocket and Blue Ghost lunar landers, and is developing a larger rocket with Northrop Grumman. It listed on Nasdaq in 2025.
revenue: NASA, the Defense Department and satellite companies pay it to launch payloads and to deliver cargo to the Moon. It also earns money building spacecraft and rocket hardware for other companies.
segments: Launch (Alpha, Eclipse) · Lunar landers (Blue Ghost) · Spacecraft · Defense

about: Runs bases, logistics, aircraft maintenance and training for the US military and allied governments. It was formed in 2022 when Vectrus merged with Vertex Aerospace.
revenue: Nearly all of its sales come from government contracts, many of them multi-year, to operate and maintain bases, equipment and aircraft. It is paid for the services and people it supplies under each task order.
segments: Base operations and logistics · Aircraft maintenance · Training and readiness · Communications and IT

about: An independent aviation services company that supplies aircraft parts and repairs and maintains aircraft for airlines and the US government.
revenue: It sells new and used aircraft parts, overhauls aircraft and components in its repair shops, and runs supply-chain and logistics programs for military customers. Airlines and defense agencies are its main customers.
segments: Parts supply · Repair and engineering · Integrated solutions · Expeditionary services

about: A US exporter of liquefied natural gas with two export plants in Louisiana, Calcasieu Pass and Plaquemines, and a third, CP2, being built. It listed on the NYSE in 2025.
revenue: It buys natural gas, chills it into liquid and ships it abroad. Most of its output is sold under long-term contracts to utilities and energy companies, and the rest as single cargoes at market prices.
segments: Calcasieu Pass · Plaquemines LNG · CP2 (under construction) · Shipping

about: Builds parts and systems for spacecraft, such as roll-out solar arrays, antennas, cameras and docking hardware. Since 2025 it also makes military drones through Edge Autonomy.
revenue: NASA, the Defense Department and commercial satellite builders pay it under contracts to design and deliver space hardware. Its drone business sells small uncrewed aircraft to defense customers.
segments: Space infrastructure · Spacecraft components · Uncrewed aircraft (Edge Autonomy)

about: Makes Orladeyo, a daily pill that prevents attacks of hereditary angioedema, a rare swelling disorder, and develops treatments for other rare diseases.
revenue: Nearly all of its sales come from Orladeyo, mainly in the US. It also earns some royalties and partnership fees.
segments: Orladeyo (hereditary angioedema) · Rare-disease pipeline

about: Argentina's largest independent energy company. It generates electricity and produces natural gas and oil, much of it from the Vaca Muerta shale. Its shares trade in New York as ADRs.
revenue: It sells power to Argentina's grid and large customers, sells gas and oil from its fields, and makes petrochemicals. It also earns income from stakes in Argentina's main gas pipeline company (TGS) and power transmission company (Transener).
segments: Power generation · Oil and gas · Petrochemicals · Pipeline and transmission stakes

about: One of the largest US power companies. It owns gas, coal and nuclear power plants, mostly in Texas and the eastern US, and sells electricity to millions of homes under brands such as Reliant.
revenue: Most of its money comes from selling electricity and natural gas to homes and businesses on retail plans. Its plants also sell power and capacity into wholesale markets, and it sells smart-home security through Vivint.
segments: Retail electricity · Power generation · Smart home (Vivint)

about: An oilfield services company that works almost entirely in the Middle East and North Africa, with Saudi Aramco and other national oil companies as its main clients.
revenue: National oil companies pay it to drill, test and maintain wells and to pump fracturing and stimulation treatments, under multi-year service contracts.
segments: Production services · Drilling and evaluation services

about: Makes NAND flash memory chips and the drives built from them, from data-center SSDs to memory cards. It was spun off from Western Digital in February 2025.
revenue: It sells flash chips and solid-state drives to data-center operators, PC and phone makers, and consumers. Flash prices swing with supply and demand, so its profits rise and fall with the memory cycle.
segments: Data-center SSDs · PC and phone storage · Consumer storage (cards and USB drives)

about: Makes heating and cooling equipment. Its fastest-growing line is cooling systems for data centers; it also makes heat-transfer parts for vehicles and industrial machines.
revenue: It sells chillers, air handlers and other cooling gear to companies that build and run data centers, plus heating and ventilation equipment for schools and commercial buildings. Truck, bus and machinery makers buy its radiators and heat exchangers.
segments: Climate Solutions (data-center cooling, HVAC) · Performance Technologies (vehicle and industrial)

about: Develops RNA-targeted (antisense) medicines. It sells Tryngolza for a rare blood-fat disorder and Dawnzera for hereditary angioedema, and helped create Spinraza for spinal muscular atrophy.
revenue: It earns product sales from its own drugs, royalties on drugs it developed with partners, such as Biogen's Spinraza and AstraZeneca's Wainua, and fees from research partnerships.
segments: Own medicines · Royalties · Partnered research

about: Makes the gas and liquid delivery systems that go inside chip-making machines.
revenue: It sells these subsystems and precision parts to equipment makers such as Lam Research and Applied Materials, so its sales track how much chipmakers spend on new equipment.
segments: Gas delivery systems · Liquid delivery systems · Machined and plastic parts

about: A Brazilian digital bank (Banco Inter) whose single app covers banking, investing, insurance and shopping. It has no branches.
revenue: It earns interest on mortgages, payroll-deducted loans, credit cards and business loans, plus fees from card spending, investments, insurance and commissions on its in-app marketplace.
segments: Banking and lending · Investments · Insurance · In-app shopping

about: Designs the Xe-100, a small modular nuclear reactor cooled by helium, and makes the TRISO pellet fuel it runs on. Its first plant is planned at a Dow chemical site in Texas.
revenue: So far most of its money comes from government cost-sharing awards and engineering work for customers such as Dow and Amazon. Selling reactors, fuel and services is still ahead of it.
segments: Xe-100 reactors · TRISO-X fuel · Engineering services

about: A clinical-stage drug developer making pills that act on cell-surface receptors (GPCRs). Its lead drug, aleniglipron, is an oral GLP-1 for obesity.
revenue: It has no approved products, so it has no sales yet. It pays for its trials with cash raised from investors.
segments: Oral GLP-1 (obesity) · Other metabolic and lung programs

about: Develops treatments for urologic cancers that avoid surgery. It sells Jelmyto for a rare upper-tract cancer and Zusduri for a common low-grade form of bladder cancer.
revenue: Its sales come from Jelmyto and Zusduri, which urologists give in their clinics and hospitals buy. It is still working toward its first profitable quarter.
segments: Jelmyto · Zusduri · Pipeline

about: One of the largest infrastructure consulting firms in the world. It designs and manages projects such as transit systems, water works, bridges and government facilities for public agencies and companies.
revenue: Clients pay it fees for engineering, design, program management and advisory work, much of it under multi-year contracts with US and foreign governments. It has moved away from building projects itself to focus on higher-margin professional services.
segments: Transportation · Water and environment · Facilities · Program management · Advisory

about: Makes electrical distribution equipment, including low- and medium-voltage switchgear and substation, padmount and dry-type transformers, for data centers, utility grids and industrial sites. It listed on the NYSE in February 2026.
revenue: It sells the equipment that steps down and routes power inside data centers, plants and utility sites, much of it built to order against a backlog of contracted projects. Data-center builders are a large source of demand.
segments: Switchgear · Transformers · Power distribution

about: Makes software and devices that police, prosecutors and government agencies use to extract and analyse data from phones and computers during investigations.
revenue: Most revenue comes from subscriptions and licenses sold to law enforcement and government agencies around the world, with some sales to companies for internal investigations. Customers renew each year, so revenue is largely recurring.
segments: Digital forensics (data collection and review) · Investigative analytics · Case management

about: Makes medicines from donated blood plasma, mainly immune globulins that protect people with weak immune systems from infection. It runs its own plasma collection centers.
revenue: Most sales come from its immune globulin products, led by Asceniv and Bivigam, sold to hospitals, specialty pharmacies and infusion centers. It also sells some of the plasma it collects to other drugmakers.
segments: Asceniv · Bivigam · Nabi-HB · Plasma collection

about: A specialty insurer and reinsurer that covers complex business risks such as professional liability, cyber, marine, energy and property.
revenue: It collects premiums for the risks it underwrites and earns investment income on the money it holds until claims are paid. Profit depends on pricing policies above the claims that come in later, so its reserve estimates matter.
segments: Specialty insurance · Reinsurance

about: A drugmaker focused on brain and nervous-system disorders. It sells Nuplazid for hallucinations and delusions in Parkinson's disease and Daybue for Rett syndrome.
revenue: Almost all revenue comes from sales of its two approved drugs, mostly in the US. It spends much of the profit on trials of new drugs for neurological and psychiatric conditions.
segments: Nuplazid · Daybue · Pipeline

about: Formerly Nextracker, the largest maker of solar trackers, the motorised mounts that turn utility-scale solar panels to follow the sun. It renamed itself Nextpower in late 2025 as it added other power-plant equipment.
revenue: It sells tracker systems, plus software, foundations and electrical gear, to developers and builders of large solar farms, mostly in the US. Revenue is booked as projects are delivered from its backlog.
segments: Solar trackers · Software and services · Foundations and electrical equipment

about: Makes the automated equipment chipmakers use to test semiconductors, including AI processors and memory, before they ship. It also makes collaborative and mobile robots.
revenue: Most revenue comes from selling and servicing chip-testing systems to chipmakers and contract manufacturers, so it rises and falls with their production plans. Its robotics arm, Universal Robots and MiR, sells robots to factories and warehouses.
segments: Semiconductor test · Product test · Robotics

about: A drug developer working on treatments for obesity and metabolic disease, led by VK2735, a GLP-1 drug being tested as an injection and as a pill. It has no approved products.
revenue: It has no product sales. It pays for its trials with cash raised from investors, and any future revenue depends on approval and launch of its obesity drugs or a deal with a larger drugmaker.
segments: VK2735 (obesity, injection and pill) · VK2809 (liver disease) · Pipeline

about: A cancer drugmaker with two approved medicines: Revuforj, a menin inhibitor for certain acute leukemias, and Niktimvo, for chronic graft-versus-host disease.
revenue: It earns product sales of Revuforj and a share of Niktimvo's profits through its partner Incyte. It is still spending heavily to widen the drugs' approved uses.
segments: Revuforj (revumenib) · Niktimvo (axatilimab) · Pipeline

about: Engineers, installs and maintains the mechanical, electrical and energy-efficiency systems in buildings such as data centers, hospitals, labs and factories. Backed by Blackstone, it listed on Nasdaq in September 2025.
revenue: Clients pay it for engineering and consulting work, for installing cooling, heating and other building systems, and for ongoing maintenance contracts. Much of the work is booked into a multi-year backlog.
segments: Engineering and consulting · Installation and maintenance

about: Makes inspection and measurement machines that chipmakers use to check wafers for defects, especially in advanced packaging such as the high-bandwidth memory and chiplets inside AI chips.
revenue: It sells its inspection and metrology systems, plus service, to chipmakers and packaging houses, mostly in Asia. Muse's Nov 18 post puts advanced packaging at about 80% of revenue.
segments: Advanced packaging inspection · Metrology · Compound semiconductors

about: A drug developer focused on epilepsy and movement disorders such as essential tremor, with drugs that target the brain's ion channels.
revenue: It has no product sales yet and funds its research with cash raised from investors. Future revenue depends on approval and launch of its first drugs; Muse's Nov 18 post mentions FDA decisions due Dec 27 and Jan 29.
segments: Essential tremor · Epilepsy · Pipeline

hq: New York, New York (some profiles say San Francisco)
about: A lender and loan marketplace built on its own blockchain, Provenance. It originates, sells and services loans, mainly home-equity lines of credit, for itself and for partner lenders, and listed on Nasdaq in September 2025.
revenue: It earns fees when loans are originated and sold through its platform and its Figure Connect marketplace, plus servicing and technology fees from partners. Growth depends on how much loan volume flows through the marketplace.
segments: Home-equity lending · Figure Connect marketplace · Partner technology · Provenance blockchain

about: Makes enclosures, electrical connection and protection products, and thermal-management gear, including liquid-cooling systems for data-center servers.
revenue: It sells through distributors and directly to builders of data centers, utilities, factories and commercial buildings. Data-center cooling and power products have been driving its growth.
segments: Systems protection (enclosures and cooling) · Electrical connections

about: Designs the controller chips that manage NAND flash memory in solid-state drives, phones, memory cards and data-center storage.
revenue: It sells controllers to flash-memory makers and drive brands, which pair them with NAND chips. Sales rise and fall with flash demand and the move to faster drives for PCs and AI servers.
segments: SSD controllers · Embedded storage controllers · Enterprise storage

about: Runs online auctions for used, damaged and salvage vehicles, most of them cars that insurers have written off after accidents or storms.
revenue: It earns fees from sellers, mainly insurance companies, for storing and auctioning their vehicles, and fees from buyers on each sale. Its volume depends on how many cars insurers declare total losses.
segments: US auctions · International auctions

about: Owns Progressive Leasing, which lets shoppers with weak credit take home furniture, appliances and electronics on lease-to-own plans at partner retailers, and Four Technologies, a buy-now-pay-later app.
revenue: It buys the goods from retailers and leases them to customers, collecting lease payments that add up to more than the item's price. Losses from customers who stop paying are its main risk.
segments: Progressive Leasing · Four Technologies (buy now, pay later)

about: A bank holding company whose bank, based in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, works behind the scenes for fintech companies, issuing their debit and prepaid cards and holding their customers' deposits. It also lends against vehicle fleets and real estate.
revenue: It earns fees on the card programs and accounts it runs for fintech partners, and interest on its loans, which are funded by the low-cost deposits those partners bring in.
segments: Fintech solutions (payments and cards) · Institutional banking · Commercial fleet leasing · Real estate bridge lending

about: An online lender to consumers and small businesses that many banks don't serve, through brands such as CashNetUSA, NetCredit and OnDeck.
revenue: It earns interest and fees on instalment loans, lines of credit and small-business loans, all made online using its own credit models. Losses on loans that go bad are its main cost, so results swing with the credit health of its borrowers.
segments: Consumer lending (CashNetUSA, NetCredit) · Small business lending (OnDeck, Headway)

about: Designs display driver chips for TVs, laptops, phones and car screens, plus image sensors and optics used in augmented-reality devices.
revenue: Most revenue comes from selling display driver and timing-controller chips to panel makers, with car displays a large share. Newer lines in AR optics and optical links for AI servers are still small.
segments: Display drivers · Timing controllers · Automotive displays · AR optics and sensing

about: A South Korean memory-chip maker and, with Samsung and Micron, one of three companies that supply most of the world's DRAM. It is the leading supplier of the high-bandwidth memory stacked next to AI accelerators. SKHY is its US listing on Nasdaq, quoted in dollars; the Seoul shares trade as 000660.KS.
revenue: It sells memory chips by the wafer-load to server builders, phone makers and AI chip companies. Prices swing hard with supply and demand, so profits can move far more than revenue; the high-bandwidth memory used in AI systems is sold out well ahead on contract.
segments: DRAM · High-bandwidth memory · NAND flash

about: An NYSE-listed maker of subsystems for space and defense programs. Its exchange profile lists three markets: aerospace and launch systems, defense aviation and airborne systems, and C5ISR and precision-strike systems.
revenue: It sells subsystems and components into government space and defense programs, so revenue follows contract awards. Gemini's Nov 18 post cites a record $1.26B backlog; its revenue mix has not been checked against company filings for this entry.
segments: Aerospace and launch systems · Defense aviation and airborne systems · C5ISR and precision strike

about: Runs StubHub and viagogo, online marketplaces where fans buy and resell tickets to concerts, sports and theater. It listed on the NYSE in September 2025.
revenue: It takes fees from buyers and sellers on each ticket sold, so revenue tracks the value of tickets traded on its sites. It also sells some tickets directly for venues and teams.
segments: StubHub (North America) · viagogo (international) · Direct ticket sales

about: A leading US uranium producer that runs the White Mesa Mill in Utah, the only working conventional uranium mill in the country. It also processes rare earth elements and owns mineral-sands projects.
revenue: It sells uranium concentrate to nuclear utilities under contracts and on the spot market, and vanadium when prices allow. Rare earth oxides used in magnets are a newer, growing line.
segments: Uranium · Rare earth elements · Vanadium · Heavy mineral sands

about: A space company that builds and flies robotic lunar landers and runs data and navigation services for missions to the Moon, much of it for NASA.
revenue: Most revenue comes from NASA and other government contracts for lunar delivery missions, lunar rovers and deep-space communications. It is lumpy because it is booked as large missions progress.
segments: Lunar access (landers) · Data transmission and navigation · Infrastructure services

about: An AI company that builds the Claude family of large language models and sells access to them. Its shares began trading on Nasdaq on Nov 19, 2026.
revenue: Most revenue comes from businesses and developers paying to use Claude through its API, directly or through cloud partners such as Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud. Subscriptions to the Claude apps (individual, team and enterprise plans) and its coding tool, Claude Code, make up much of the rest.
segments: API and cloud platforms · Claude app subscriptions · Claude Code · Enterprise

about: Designs processors and graphics chips: EPYC server CPUs, Instinct AI accelerators, Ryzen PC processors and Radeon graphics. Manufacturing is outsourced, mostly to TSMC.
revenue: Data-center chips (server CPUs and Instinct AI accelerators) are the largest and fastest-growing business, followed by PC processors. Gaming chips, including the ones inside PlayStation and Xbox consoles, and embedded chips from its Xilinx purchase make up the rest.
segments: Data center · Client (PCs) · Gaming · Embedded

about: A 'neocloud': it rents out large clusters of Nvidia GPUs in its own data centers to AI labs and big tech companies.
revenue: Customers sign multi-year contracts for GPU computing capacity. A handful of large customers, such as Microsoft and OpenAI, account for most revenue, and the build-out is funded heavily with debt.
segments: GPU cloud for AI training and inference · Storage and networking · Managed software

about: Google's parent company: Search, YouTube, Android, Chrome and Google Cloud, plus the Gemini AI models and the Waymo self-driving business.
revenue: Mostly advertising on Google Search and YouTube. Google Cloud (computing, data and AI services for businesses) is the second engine; subscriptions, Play store fees and devices add the rest.
segments: Search ads · YouTube · Google Cloud · Subscriptions and devices · Other Bets (Waymo)

about: Builds and launches rockets and spacecraft (Falcon 9, Dragon, Starship) and runs Starlink, the largest satellite-internet network. Cramer's Nov 19 posts say it also rents out AI computing capacity to Anthropic and Google.
revenue: Starlink subscriptions and dishes are the biggest business. Launches for NASA, the US military and commercial customers, and other government contracts, make up most of the rest.
segments: Starlink · Launch services · Human spaceflight · Government contracts

about: Makes the iPhone, Mac, iPad, Apple Watch and AirPods, and runs services such as the App Store, iCloud, Apple Music and Apple Pay.
revenue: The iPhone brings in about half of sales. Services (App Store fees, subscriptions, iCloud, and Google's payments to be the default search engine) are the second-biggest and most profitable line; Macs, iPads and wearables make up the rest.
segments: iPhone · Services · Mac · iPad · Wearables and accessories

about: The maker of Windows, Microsoft 365 (Office) and the Azure cloud, and a major partner of and investor in OpenAI.
revenue: Azure cloud and server software are the biggest driver, then Microsoft 365 subscriptions for businesses and consumers. LinkedIn, Dynamics business software, Windows licenses, Xbox gaming and search ads make up the rest.
segments: Azure and server software · Microsoft 365 · LinkedIn · Dynamics · Windows and devices · Gaming

about: The biggest seller of customer-relationship-management (CRM) software for sales, service and marketing teams. It also owns Slack, Tableau and MuleSoft, and sells AI agents through Agentforce.
revenue: Almost all revenue is cloud subscriptions sold per user per year: Sales Cloud, Service Cloud, marketing and commerce tools, Slack, and data and analytics products. Professional services are a small remainder.
segments: Sales Cloud · Service Cloud · Platform and Slack · Marketing and Commerce · Integration and Analytics

about: Sells cloud software that runs IT help desks and automates company workflows, from IT and HR requests to customer service.
revenue: Nearly all revenue is subscriptions to its Now Platform, priced by users and modules and sold mainly to large companies and governments. AI add-ons are a growing piece.
segments: IT service management · IT operations · Employee workflows · Customer workflows · AI and app-building tools

about: A cybersecurity company whose Falcon platform protects laptops, servers and cloud systems from hackers, using a small software agent and cloud-based threat detection.
revenue: Annual subscriptions to Falcon modules: endpoint protection, cloud security, identity protection, threat intelligence and managed detection. A small share comes from services such as incident response.
segments: Endpoint security · Cloud security · Identity protection · Security logging (SIEM) · Services

about: Runs off-price stores that sell brand-name clothing and home goods below department-store prices: T.J. Maxx, Marshalls, HomeGoods and Sierra in the US, Winners in Canada and TK Maxx in Europe and Australia.
revenue: It buys brands' excess and closeout stock at a discount and sells it in about 5,000 stores. Marmaxx (T.J. Maxx and Marshalls) is by far the largest division.
segments: Marmaxx · HomeGoods · TJX Canada · TJX International

about: The largest home-improvement retailer, with about 2,300 stores in the US, Canada and Mexico, selling to do-it-yourself shoppers and to professional contractors.
revenue: Sales of building materials, lumber, tools, appliances and garden supplies in stores and online. It is growing its contractor business through acquired distributors such as SRS.
segments: Retail stores · Pro contractors · SRS Distribution · Online

about: The biggest maker of networking equipment (switches and routers) for companies, telecom carriers and data centers, plus security, observability (Splunk) and collaboration (Webex) software.
revenue: Hardware sales of switches, routers and wireless gear are the largest share, increasingly including AI data-center networking for cloud companies. Security and Splunk software, Webex and support services add recurring revenue.
segments: Networking · Security · Observability (Splunk) · Collaboration · Services

about: Makes wafer-scale AI chips (a single processor the size of a dinner plate) and the systems built around them, competing with Nvidia's GPUs, especially for running AI models (inference).
revenue: Sells its CS-series AI systems and, increasingly, rents out inference computing through its own cloud. A few large customers, historically Abu Dhabi's G42, have accounted for much of revenue.
segments: AI systems · Inference cloud · Support services

about: Makes the power and cooling equipment that keeps data centers running: backup power (UPS), power distribution, thermal management and liquid cooling.
revenue: Sells equipment and service contracts to cloud companies, colocation operators and telecom carriers. AI data centers, which need far more power and liquid cooling, are its fastest-growing market.
segments: Power management · Thermal management and liquid cooling · Integrated racks and modules · Services

hq: Dublin, Ireland (main US offices near Cleveland, Ohio)
about: An industrial company focused on electrical equipment (switchgear, transformers, breakers and power-distribution gear for data centers, utilities and buildings), plus aerospace and vehicle parts.
revenue: Electrical products and systems for data centers, utilities, commercial buildings and homes make up most sales. Aircraft fuel and hydraulic systems and truck and car components make up the rest.
segments: Electrical Americas · Electrical Global · Aerospace · Vehicle · eMobility

about: The largest maker of PC and server processors and one of the few chip companies that also manufactures its own chips. It is building a contract-manufacturing business, Intel Foundry, to make chips for others; the US government and Nvidia are large shareholders.
revenue: Core PC processors and Xeon server chips account for most revenue. Intel Foundry so far earns little from outside customers, and Intel also owns most of Mobileye (driver-assistance chips).
segments: Client computing (PCs) · Data center and AI · Intel Foundry · Mobileye

about: Runs about 900 membership warehouse clubs worldwide that sell groceries, household goods, electronics, gasoline and more in bulk at low markups.
revenue: Merchandise sales bring in almost all revenue at thin margins, but most of the profit comes from annual membership fees paid by tens of millions of households.
segments: Warehouse merchandise · Membership fees · Gasoline and services · E-commerce

about: DuPont's former electronics business, spun off as its own company in November 2025. It makes materials used to manufacture chips and circuit boards, such as polishing slurries and pads, photoresists and plating chemicals.
revenue: Sells consumable materials to chipmakers and to circuit-board and electronics makers, so sales track how many chips and boards are produced.
segments: Semiconductor materials (CMP, lithography) · Interconnect and packaging materials
